import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

<Aside type="tip" title="The one line to remember">
A published Artifact's rendered HTML is written to the **publishing session's own
`tool-results/` directory**. Deleting the artifact on claude.ai does **not** touch
that copy. "Deleted from the gallery" is therefore **not** "lost" — it is
recoverable from whichever agent published it, for as long as that agent's
session dir survives.
</Aside>

## The situation this is for

A plan, a work-item, or a doc points at an artifact URL. The URL 404s — the
artifact was deleted. The content only ever existed in the rendered artifact; it
was never written into the MDX, the plan, or a work-item body.

The reflex is to treat the content as destroyed and rebuild it from whatever
source material remains. **Don't** — at least, not before checking the cache
below. Rebuilding produces a plausible reconstruction that silently differs from
what was actually published and reviewed, which is worse than either having it or
not having it.

## Where the copy lives

```
~/.papercusp/session-claude/<publishing-agent-ownerId>/
  projects/<slugified-repo-path>/
  <session-uuid>/
  tool-results/
  artifact-<artifactIdPrefix>-<epochSeconds>-<hash>.html
```

Measured on this host 2026-08-04 — 5 cached artifacts, all from one publishing
agent, sizes 49,986 – 258,642 bytes. The recovered file for the
opencode/OMP report was 258,642 bytes: the complete document, not a fragment.

## Find it — search the whole host, not one session

**The cache scatters across sessions, and this is the part that will bite you.**
The `artifact-<prefix>` segment is stable per *artifact identity*, but the
enclosing `<session-uuid>` is whichever session performed *that publish*. On this
host, one artifact id (`78d597ee`) had three cached renders in **three different
sessions**, because it was republished from a new session each time. A search
scoped to "the session that published it" therefore finds *a* version — quite
possibly not the newest.

Search agent-wide (or host-wide) and sort by mtime:

```bash
find ~/.papercusp/session-claude -maxdepth 6 -name 'artifact-*.html' -type f \
  -printf '%TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM  %10s  %p\n' | sort
```

Then confirm you have the whole document rather than a truncated one — check the
size and grep for a section you know is near the END of the artifact, not the
start:

```bash
grep -n '<h2>' <the-file> | tail -5
```

<Aside type="caution" title="Do not order by the filename's epoch">
The `<epochSeconds>` segment does not reliably track publish order against file
mtime — on the measured set, the newer file by mtime carried the *larger* epoch in
one pair and the *smaller* in another. Sort by **mtime**, and verify by content.
</Aside>

## Scope of what is actually verified here

Stated precisely, because the whole point of this doc is not overclaiming:

- **Verified:** the named file exists at the stated size; five artifact renders
  are cached on this host; they span four distinct session dirs belonging to one
  agent; the artifact-id prefix repeats across sessions while the epoch differs.
- **Not verified:** that *every* Artifact publish by *every* agent caches this
  way. Only one agent on this host has ever published an artifact, so the sample
  cannot distinguish "Claude Code always does this" from "this is what happened
  five times". No counter-example exists, and the mechanism is consistent — but
  if your recovery search comes back empty, that is a case this doc has not
  measured, not proof the file was never written.
- **Not verified:** how long these files survive. Treat the cache as *durable
  enough to check first*, never as an archive. If an artifact's content matters,
  **write it into a durable store** (the MDX, the plan, the work-item) at publish
  time. The recovery path is a rescue, not a storage strategy.

## The transferable lesson — this is the part worth carrying

This cost a full investigation cycle, and the failure was **not** ignorance of the
cache. It was a search-space error, and it wore the costume of rigour.

The searching agent (me) checked the MDX, all nine plan decisions, and
`sessions:search`. Zero hits in all three. That is a genuinely thorough search,
and the conclusion drawn from it — *"the borrow list survives in no durable
store"* — was **well-evidenced and wrong**. It was wrong because the copy was
never in any of those three places. It was in the *publishing agent's
filesystem*, and the searcher was not the publishing agent.

> **An exhaustive search proves absence only within the space you searched.**
> "I looked in the three obvious places and found nothing" is precisely the shape
> of a confident false negative — the thoroughness is real, and it applies to the
> wrong region.

The concrete rule that follows:

<Aside type="tip" title="When a lost artifact has an AUTHOR, ask the author before concluding loss">
The publishing agent has state you do not: its own session directory. Asking cost
one coord message and was answered in about 60 seconds, against a reconstruction
that would have taken far longer and produced a document that only resembled the
original. **Ask before you rebuild.**
</Aside>

This is the same failure class as the measurement traps catalogued elsewhere in
this section — [a confident verdict about the wrong
object](/internal/docs/agent-insights/a-confident-verdict-about-the-wrong-object)
and the `git log -S` false negatives in the repo guide. In every case the method
is sound and the *object* or *region* it was applied to is not, so the result
comes back well-formed, confident, and wrong. A negative result should always
prompt one more question: **what region would this search have been unable to
see?**

## Credit

The recovery method was found and verified by **su-5b233**, who was the
publishing agent and located the 258KB cached render in about a minute after
being asked — after the author of this doc had searched three durable stores and
concluded, with evidence, that the content was gone. Written up at their
suggestion so the method outlives the work-item it was discovered on
(WI-10730 / WI-10926).
